offer.title: Offer layer
offer.desc: This site sells. These are the fields an assistant ranks products on, and without them an agent can talk about you but cannot send you a buyer.

layers.title: Where AI engines get their information
layers.desc: From three layers, not one. A technical audit reads one and a half of them, and it is worth knowing which.

crawled.title: Crawled data
crawled.body: Your indexed pages and what everyone else writes about you. They decide which category a model files you under, and who it compares you against.

feeds.title: Feeds and APIs
feeds.body: What you publish as structured data: prices, availability, attributes. It decides how you are compared when someone asks for a recommendation. No free audit sees this, because it lives in your feed rather than on your page.

live.title: Live site data
live.body: Real price, stock, reviews, checkout. They decide whether an agent can act on a buyer's behalf, or merely describe you.

limit.title: This audit tells you whether you can be cited, not whether you are
limit.body: Those are two different questions with two different answers. A site can pass every check on this page and never appear in a ChatGPT answer, because access is a precondition and not a cause. The only way to know whether you are cited is to ask the engines, repeatedly, and count the answers that name you.
limit.weights: In the citability model we run inside Anomalia, this technical audit carries 10% of the weight. The rest is extractability (25%), evidence density (25%), entity clarity (20%) and third-party corroboration (20%).

geo-vs-seo.q: What is GEO, and how is it different from SEO?
geo-vs-seo.a: SEO optimises for a position in a list of links; GEO optimises for being named inside a generated answer. The unit of measurement changes: not average position, but the share of answers your brand appears in. A site can rank first on Google and never be cited by ChatGPT.

proves-citation.q: Does this audit prove that ChatGPT cites me?
proves-citation.a: No. It checks that AI crawlers can read you, that structured data is present, and that the page is intelligible to a machine — the preconditions. Whether you are actually cited is a different measurement, one that requires querying the engines repeatedly and counting.

where-ai-reads.q: Where do AI engines get their information?
where-ai-reads.a: From three layers: crawled pages, the feeds and structured APIs you publish, and live site data. The three can contradict each other — a price in the feed that differs from the page — and contradiction is one of the fastest ways to stop being recommended.

product-offer.q: Does my ecommerce site need Product and Offer data?
product-offer.a: Yes, and it is the most expensive gap this audit finds. Without a Product block containing an Offer that states price, currency and availability, an assistant can describe the brand and cannot rank a single item. Add an identifier (sku, gtin) and the product URL and it can also send you a buyer.

llms-txt.a: It is an emerging standard, not a requirement: no engine has declared it a ranking factor. It costs ten minutes and hands engines a curated map of the pages that matter, so we recommend it — but it carries little weight, and if you could fix only one thing it would not be this.

what-moves-citation.a: The one controlled study in this space (Princeton, KDD 2024) measured the visibility lift of individual tactics in generative engines: direct quotations roughly +41%, statistics +33%, fluency +29%, citing sources +27%, while keyword stuffing did nothing at all. Engines have moved since; the ordering — evidence density beats keyword tactics — has held in every replication.

info.whyBody: Sites with llms.txt are more likely to be cited in AI-generated answers. It's a simple signal that you care about AI visibility.
